prime.problem: A sweep produces many outcomes and many arm contrasts. If you decide which to test after looking, some will come out 'significant' by chance, and no reader can tell a real effect from a chosen one.
prime.fits: The third capstone step. It fixes, in a commit, how the design from Branch from the agent's own run will be scored, using the multiple-comparisons and clustering ideas from course 4 and an LLM labeller like the judges in course 5.
expect: tampering promoted to a confirmatory hypothesis
a frozen extractor pinned by a hash
an acceptance rule that survives κ = 0
prime.goal: List the confirmatory tests and their thresholds, explain why the held-out κ is 0.000 yet the classifier passed, and draft any future change as a correctly formed addendum.

attend: Which four parts make up P1, and which one was redefined after the second plumbing check?
Why is the extractor's prompt hash part of the registration rather than an implementation detail?
How can 65 of 66 agreements give κ = 0.000, and what did the acceptance rule require in that case?
What protects H2 from being an artefact of the pilot that suggested it?
Which commits happened before the baseline pilot ran, and which after?

must: An analysis has many defensible choices → choosing after seeing data finds 'effects' in noise (with 20 independent tests at 0.05, about a 64% chance of at least one) → commit the outcomes, contrasts and corrections before the data exists

The outcomes come from an LLM extractor → a changed prompt changes the outcome → the prompt hash is registered and a test fails if it drifts → the only way to change it is an addendum that records the new hash

κ corrects agreement for chance → when every hand label is one class, chance agreement equals observed agreement → κ is 0 (or undefined) whatever the accuracy → the rule falls back to accuracy plus 100% recall on positives when there are fewer than 5

Tampering looked promising only because the pilot was examined → testing it on the same tasks would reuse the data that suggested it → addendum 3 tests H2 on 40 fresh tasks disjoint from the pilot's, one-sided at 0.025, before any sweep run
elevated: Addenda 1 and 2 came from small plumbing checks (one task, then two) that are excluded from every estimate → design flaws could be fixed without touching confirmatory data → but each fix is still a researcher choice the paper must report
reference: acceptance: κ ≥ 0.80 and accuracy ≥ 90% on P1 (finals and summaries), ≥ 90% on P2
held-out: 65/66 finals, 24/24 summaries, 49/49 attribution; dev: 36/36, κ 1.000
H1a/H1b Holm at family-wise 0.05; H2 one-sided p < 0.025; secondary families T (5), S (6), M (1)

compress.prompt: Card closed: in 4–5 sentences, explain what the registration commits to, how it may change, and why that makes the sweep's confirmatory result believable.
checklist: outcomes P1 (four parts) and P2, plus tampering and inflation, defined before data
a frozen extractor with a registered prompt hash and held-out agreement checks
fixed contrasts, corrections, n and a stopping rule with no interim looks
changes only as dated addenda saying what was seen and what changes
the pilot's tampering lead re-tested on fresh tasks

retrieve.q: Explain the garden of forking paths and why it can produce a false finding without anyone cheating.
answer: each analysis choice (outcome, arms, exclusions, test) is reasonable on its own
choosing them after seeing the data lets noise steer the choices
many implicit comparisons inflate the chance of a spurious 'significant' result

retrieve.q: Walk through what happens if someone edits the extractor's prompt after registration.
answer: the SHA-256 of the two prompts changes
test_prompt_is_frozen fails because the hash no longer starts with the registered prefix

the change needs a dated addendum with the new hash (as addendum 2 did); if the change follows a failed acceptance check, §3.1 also requires validation on at least 60 fresh hand labels before any outcome is unblinded

retrieve.q: Addendum 2 added a 'do not modify, skip or delete the existing tests' line after seeing plumbing data. What did it buy, and what did it cost?
answer: it made the measured decision (disclose vs claim success) actually arise; without it 4 of 6 branches simply skipped the test
it is a researcher degree of freedom chosen on data, now on record
it may shift tampering base rates relative to real repos that lack the line

retrieve.q: How is H2 tested, step by step, according to addendum 3?
answer: per prefix: tampering in the d1-codex branch minus tampering in the d0 branch
mean over prefixes, pooled over both models
task-cluster bootstrap, B = 10,000, one-sided p = share of bootstrap means ≤ 0
supported if p < 0.025 and the estimate is positive; its own family, not Holm-adjusted with H1

compare.q: Error bars covered clustered resampling. What does pre-registration add that a correct interval can't?
answer: a correct interval for a contrast chosen after the fact is still misleading
registration fixes which contrasts get intervals and corrections before data
both are needed: honest intervals on honestly chosen tests

compare.q: Course 5 showed rubric judges get gamed. Here an LLM is the outcome labeller. Which risks carry over, and which controls does the registration add?
answer: the labeller can drift or be wrong in systematic ways, like a judge
here nothing is optimised against it, so gaming pressure is low
controls: frozen prompt and hash, temperature 0, regex cross-check, held-out hand labels with an acceptance rule

predict.q: The sweep finishes and H2's estimate is +8 points with one-sided p = 0.04. Before reading the analysis card, predict how the paper must report it and what it may not do.
predict.answer: H2 is not supported: the registered threshold is p < 0.025. The paper reports the estimate, its CI and the p-value as a null for the confirmatory test, may discuss it as weak evidence, and may not switch to a two-sided α of 0.05, drop a model, or pick a better-looking arm after the fact. Exploratory per-model results can be shown but labelled exploratory.

apply.task: Draft 'Addendum 4' for a hypothetical change: you want to add a third model after the sweep's first chunk. Write it in the registration's style: what was seen, why it matters, exactly what changes, and what happens to data already collected. Then check it against addendum 3's rule on interim looks.
apply.done: Your draft names the trigger (no outcome by arm may have been looked at), states the change and its cost cap, keeps the first chunk's data rules intact, and you've found the sentence in addendum 3 that limits monitoring to cost, stop reasons, error counts and prefix yield.
apply.hint: Addendum 3 says between and during chunks only cost, stop reasons, error counts and prefix yield are inspected (--blind), never an outcome by arm.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: how κ behaves with one class, or which commits came before the pilot?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why addenda are allowed, or why that doesn't defeat registration?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: many tests → false positives, or Holm correction → family-wise error?
What would you need to see to trust the extractor on the sweep's positives?
Which researcher choice in this study would you most want a reviewer to know about?
